To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
humans can be redirected by 49 percent in the rotation task, 26 percent in the downscaled distance task, and 22 m in the curvature task.

1) users can be redirected about 49 percent in the case of rotations; 2) distances can be scaled about 26 percent in the case that the virtual world is larger than the real world; and 3) the radius of the circular arc can be 22 m.
humans can unknowingly walk through a virtual world that is 49% larger than the physical world, and that the virtual world can be up to 22% longer than the physical world.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question how far users can be redirected from their physical paths without being aware of it.
the quantification of human perception of virtual reality (VR) motion in the real world.
the question of how much users can be unknowingly redirected on paths that are different than the visually perceived paths.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
users can be redirected by up to 50% in the direction of the physical movement and by up to 26% of the distance in the direction of visual motion.
humans are very good in discriminating between physical and virtual rotations and straightforward movements, but are very bad at discriminating between physical curvature and virtual straightness.
humans are able to detect a redirected walk when it is greater than 20 percent in any direction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
users can be redirected up to 50 percent in all three tested directions.

the detection thresholds of the three tested redirection techniques depend on the magnitude of the gain and that the detection threshold for redirection in the horizontal plane is smaller than in the vertical plane.

users can be redirected up to 50 percent in all directions and up to 26 percent along the forward direction, while they believe that the virtual environment moves in accordance with their physical movements.
The main takeaway from our work is that
humans have a remarkable tolerance to be physically redirected in IVEs.
redirection gains can be much larger than previously reported.
users are not very accurate in detecting redirections and that the thresholds are dependent on the type of redirection.
